_about: PRO rewrite pass 4: era-1 scenes 118-150 in play order.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Who Talks Too Much
scenarios.text: A rookie in your class keeps posting locker-room jokes online: who fell asleep in meetings, who cried at a movie on the plane. The veterans are getting angry, and they've noticed you sit with him.

choices.label: Talk to him privately
choices.result: A quiet word in the parking lot. He genuinely didn't know it was a big deal, deletes four posts on the spot and buys the veterans breakfast on Friday.

choices.label: Let a veteran handle it
choices.result: A veteran you trust hears it from you, and handles it better than you could have: one sentence in the weight room, and the posts stop.

choices.label: Let him learn the hard way
choices.result: Not your fight, you decide. The veterans handle it loudly, with a whole-team meeting, and the rookie doesn't speak to anyone for a week.

scenarios.title: The Specialist Meeting Room
scenarios.text: The specialists' meeting room is the size of a closet, with a broken projector, one working outlet and a mop bucket nobody has moved since September. Three of you share it every morning.

choices.label: Ask for a real room
choices.result: The operations staff gets a polite, specific request from you, with a floor plan. You get a real room by Monday, and the punter calls you a hero for a month.

choices.label: Make the closet great
choices.result: Snacks, a better extension cord and a lamp from home. The closet becomes the best room in the building, and the linebackers start asking to visit.

choices.label: Use the film room at night
choices.result: The main film room after hours, empty and quiet. You learn more alone there in a week than in a month of closet mornings.

scenarios.title: The Wrong Bus
scenarios.text: After a road practice you get on the wrong team bus, fall asleep, and wake up alone at the airport cargo terminal. Your phone is at four percent, and the team plane leaves in three hours.

choices.label: Post it in the group chat
choices.result: A photo of you alone at the cargo terminal goes to the group chat. The nickname 'Freight' sticks for a whole season, and you secretly love it.

choices.label: Call the travel staff
choices.result: Four percent is enough for one call to the travel staff, who send a car. You're back before anyone notices, except the travel director, who never forgets.

choices.label: Wait with a book
choices.result: Three hours with a paperback and a vending-machine dinner until the team arrives. Nobody believes your story, and the snapper still brings it up.

scenarios.title: Your First Billboard
scenarios.text: Your face goes up on a billboard by the highway for a local bank, forty feet wide, smiling a smile you don't remember making. You drive past it twice on the way to practice.

choices.label: Send a photo home
choices.result: A photo from the shoulder goes to {parent}, who drives three hours just to stand under it and take his own. He frames it for the hallway.

choices.label: Take a different road
choices.result: A different route to practice, every day. It's too strange to look at your own face that big, and you feel silly about it.

choices.label: Earn the billboard
choices.result: Billboards are for people who've earned them, you decide, and you kick an extra hundred balls that week to start.

scenarios.title: The Veteran's Retirement Party
scenarios.text: A veteran you barely know is retiring after eleven seasons, and the whole team is expected at the party in a hotel ballroom. He has never said more than three words to you.

choices.label: Listen to the stories
choices.result: An evening of stories at the back table: the old coaches, the cut days, the plays nobody filmed. You learn more about the league in one night than in a month.

choices.label: Stop by briefly
choices.result: Half an hour, a handshake and a congratulations. He remembers your name, which surprises you both, and you're home by nine.

choices.label: Toast for the rookies
choices.result: A short toast on behalf of the rookies, written on a napkin at the table. The veteran shakes your hand for a long time afterward.

scenarios.title: The Mentor Who Leaves
scenarios.text: The veteran who took you under his wing in camp is traded on a Tuesday night. By Wednesday morning his locker is empty and his name is off the parking spot.

choices.label: Help him pack the car
choices.result: His car, packed at midnight, with you carrying the heavy boxes. You keep in touch every week, and he texts you after every one of your games.

choices.label: Take his place in the room
choices.result: For the next rookie, you start doing exactly what he did for you: lunch, film, the long talks. It's the best way to thank him.

choices.label: Kick the sting out
choices.result: The sting goes into extra work that afternoon. It helps, a little, and you still look at his empty locker every morning.

scenarios.title: The Agent's Other Rookies
scenarios.text: Your agent has four rookie clients, and from how long your calls take to be returned, you can tell you're fourth. The last text you got was a thumbs-up to a question.

choices.label: Ask for a written plan
choices.result: A written plan and a monthly call, requested politely and firmly. You get both, and your agent starts calling first.

choices.label: Be impossible to ignore
choices.result: The client who's impossible to ignore, that's the plan, and you kick like it all month. Your agent calls in October to say the club asked about you.

choices.label: Let it ride
choices.result: Rookie contracts are fixed anyway, you reason, and let it ride. It's fine for now, and you wonder about next year.

scenarios.title: The Practice Squad Promotion
scenarios.text: {backup}, your friend from the practice squad, is promoted to the active roster on Thursday. They find out in the hallway and call you before they call home.

choices.label: Take them to dinner
choices.result: Dinner, your treat, at the place with the good steaks. {backup} cries at the table, and so do you, a little, into your water.

choices.label: Introduce them around
choices.result: Every veteran you know, introduced by name. {backup} fits in by the end of the week, and the room starts calling you two a package deal.

choices.label: Text congratulations
choices.result: A congratulations text, and an early night. {backup} replies with eleven exclamation points and a photo of the new locker, and doesn't sleep at all.

scenarios.title: The Bad Haircut
scenarios.text: The rookies get haircuts from the veterans, whether they want them or not. There's a folding chair in the middle of the locker room, a pair of clippers and a line.

choices.label: Volunteer to go first
choices.result: First in the chair, by choice. It's terrible, a stripe down the middle, and you wear it proudly for a month while the veterans take photos.

choices.label: Negotiate a better cut
choices.result: A less terrible haircut, negotiated in exchange for carrying the pads for a week. The veterans respect the deal more than the hair.

choices.label: Hide in the training room
choices.result: The training room, behind the cold tub. They find you anyway in ten minutes, and your haircut is worse for the delay.

scenarios.title: The Family Group Chat
scenarios.text: Your family group chat has become a running commentary on your career, including every miss in every practice clip anyone posts, with {parent} giving technical notes.

choices.label: Roast yourself first
choices.result: You join in and roast yourself before anyone else can. The chat becomes the best part of your week, and {sibling} makes you a highlight reel of your worst kicks.

choices.label: Set one rule
choices.result: One rule for the chat: no football after nine. Everyone sleeps better, and {parent} breaks it exactly once, for a good reason.

choices.label: Mute it for the season
choices.result: Muted until the season ends. {parent} is offended for a week and then sends you a long letter, on paper.

scenarios.title: The Fantasy Football Message
scenarios.text: A stranger messages you at midnight about his fantasy team. He is very angry that you only kicked one field goal, and he has a lot of opinions about your hips.

choices.label: Reply with a joke
choices.result: A reply: you'll try harder for his team specifically. He becomes your biggest fan, buys your jersey and sends you a photo in it.

choices.label: Leave it unanswered
choices.result: Unanswered, and there will be more. You go to sleep, and he messages twice more before morning, then never again.

choices.label: Block strangers' messages
choices.result: Blocked, and messages from strangers turned off entirely. Your phone goes quiet at night for the first time since the draft.

scenarios.title: Your First Credit Card Bill
scenarios.text: Your first credit card statement as a pro arrives, four pages long, and you don't remember half the charges. One of them is a subscription to a magazine about boats.

choices.label: Go through every line
choices.result: Every line, with a highlighter, at the kitchen table. Four subscriptions canceled, including the boat magazine, which you still don't remember ordering.

choices.label: Pay it and forget it
choices.result: Paid in full, and forgotten. The same thing happens next month, and the month after, with slightly different boats, and you stop opening the envelopes.

choices.label: Ask a veteran at lunch
choices.result: A veteran at lunch shows you the app he uses and his worst statement ever, which makes yours look like a grocery list. You laugh until it hurts.

scenarios.title: The Gym Membership
scenarios.text: A fancy downtown gym offers you a free membership if you post about it twice a month. It has cold plunges, a juice bar and a kicking net on the roof.

choices.label: Take it and train there
choices.result: Accepted, posted twice, and you train there all offseason. The equipment is incredible, and the rooftop net has a view of the whole city.

choices.label: Stay with the club's staff
choices.result: The club's facility, where the staff knows your body. It's less glamorous, and nobody there asks you to post anything.

choices.label: Get the rookies in too
choices.result: The rookie class gets memberships too, at your request. You all train there together, and the juice bar never recovers.

scenarios.title: The Kicking Coach From College
scenarios.text: Your college kicking coach calls: he'll be in town next week and wants to come watch a practice. He's the one who taught you everything, and he hasn't seen you kick in a year.

choices.label: Get him a pass
choices.result: A pass, a seat by the field, and he watches every single kick. His notes run three pages, and one of them fixes your short game.

choices.label: Send him film instead
choices.result: Film sent by email, and his notes come back by morning, just as sharp. He signs off 'proud of you', which you read twice.

choices.label: Not this season
choices.result: This season isn't a good time, you explain. He understands completely, and you feel bad about it every time you see a whistle.

scenarios.title: The Cold-Weather City
scenarios.text: Your first winter in a cold-weather city. It's nine degrees at practice, the ball feels like a rock, and the veterans are wearing shorts to prove a point.

choices.label: Kick outside every day
choices.result: Outside every day, whatever the temperature. By December you've stopped noticing the cold, and the ball stops feeling like a rock.

choices.label: Learn the equipment tricks
choices.result: How do they keep balls warm on the sideline? The equipment staff shows you every trick, legal and almost-legal, over hot chocolate.

choices.label: Build a warm-up routine
choices.result: A warm-up routine that keeps your leg loose between kicks: bands, a heated bench, two layers you can strip off. It's half the battle.

scenarios.title: The Hot-Weather Road Game
scenarios.text: A road game in a city where it's ninety degrees in December. The practice field is shimmering, the trainers are handing out salt tablets, and your cleats are sticking to the turf.

choices.label: Follow the hydration plan
choices.result: The trainer's hydration plan, to the letter, down to the ounce. You feel great all week while two linemen end up on IVs.

choices.label: Save your energy
choices.result: Every ounce of energy, saved: shade between drills, no extra kicks, a cold towel on your neck. You're fresh on game day.

choices.label: Kick in the heat
choices.result: Midday kicks, on purpose, to get used to it. You're exhausted, and your leg knows exactly how the ball flies in thick air.

scenarios.title: The Long Flight
scenarios.text: A five-hour flight to a road game, and the veterans play cards the whole way in the back, loudly, with a scoreboard taped to a seat.

choices.label: Watch and learn the game
choices.result: Watching, then learning the rules, then playing for matchsticks. By landing you know every veteran's story and lose very gracefully.

choices.label: Sleep all five hours
choices.result: Eye mask, earplugs and five hours of real sleep. You land fresh and rested, and the card players land looking like they've been through a war.

choices.label: Learn the stadium
choices.result: The scouting report, twice, and the stadium's wind charts. You know every flag on that field before the wheels touch down, and {coach} quizzes you on the bus.

scenarios.title: The Jersey Number
scenarios.text: You don't get the number you wore in college: a veteran linebacker has it, and he's had it for eight years. The equipment manager hands you a list of what's left.

choices.label: Pick a new one and let it go
choices.result: A new number, no fuss. The linebacker hears about it and thanks you, and gives you his old practice jersey as a joke.

choices.label: Pick a number with meaning
choices.result: Your birthday, from the list. It feels strange for a month and like yours by October, and {parent} buys the jersey first.

choices.label: Make the new number famous
choices.result: The new number is going to mean something, you decide, and you write it on your kicking tee. Every practice feels like a down payment.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Quiz
scenarios.text: The coaches give the rookies a written quiz on the club's history: championships, legends, the year the stadium roof blew off. It's Friday, and nobody told you there'd be a quiz.

choices.label: Study all week
choices.result: The club's history, studied every night. You ace the quiz, and the coaches start telling you stories nobody else gets.

choices.label: Study in a group
choices.result: A study group in the hotel lounge, with flashcards and pizza. Everyone passes, and the rookie class has its first inside joke.

choices.label: Wing it
choices.result: Winged, and half right. The veterans laugh at your answer about the stadium roof for the rest of the season, and you laugh with them.

scenarios.title: The Holiday Away From Home
scenarios.text: Your first holiday away from your family: a hotel near the stadium, a room-service menu and a phone full of photos from the dinner table at home.

choices.label: Join dinner by video
choices.result: A video call into the family dinner, propped up on the table between the potatoes. It's silly and wonderful, and {sibling} feeds the phone a bite.

choices.label: Gather the stranded rookies
choices.result: The rookies who can't go home, gathered in the hotel restaurant for a long dinner. It becomes a tradition, and you run it every year after.

choices.label: Rest and watch movies
choices.result: Room service and three movies in a row. It's quiet and restful and a little sad, and you call home twice.

scenarios.title: The Team Thanksgiving
scenarios.text: A veteran and his family host a holiday dinner for the young players who can't go home: long tables in his backyard, his grandmother's recipes, and kids running everywhere.

choices.label: Go early and help cook
choices.result: Early, with an apron. The veteran's grandmother adopts you for the night, teaches you her stuffing and sends you home with leftovers.

choices.label: Eat and go home happy
choices.result: Dinner, far too much of it, and home happy by nine. It's the best meal you've had since camp, and you sleep like a stone.

choices.label: Bring a dish from home
choices.result: {parent}'s recipe, cooked badly, and the story behind it. The table goes quiet while you tell it, and somebody asks for seconds.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Baby
scenarios.text: A teammate's baby is born on a game week, in the middle of the night, and the whole locker room is celebrating with a cake shaped like a football and a banner made of tape.

choices.label: Organize a team gift
choices.result: A team gift, organized by you: a tiny jersey with every player's signature. The teammate tears up at his locker and can't speak.

choices.label: Congratulate him and work
choices.result: A congratulations and a hug, then back to your routine. He's grateful, and he's not thinking about anyone's routine this week.

choices.label: Cover his meeting notes
choices.result: His special teams meeting notes, covered by you all week, so he can stay home. He comes back to a binder with his name on it.

scenarios.title: The Old College Rival
scenarios.text: A kicker you competed against all through college has signed with a club in your division. You'll be on the same field twice a year, and the local paper has already noticed.

choices.label: Text him before the first game
choices.result: A text the week before your first game against his club. You have dinner afterward and laugh about the college stuff that once felt huge.

choices.label: Use the rivalry
choices.result: Fuel, all week: the old rivalry gives every practice a little extra. He doesn't know, and you don't tell him.

choices.label: Study his film
choices.result: His film, studied closely, and you learn something about your own hips from the way he sets up. You send him a thank-you he doesn't understand.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Hazing Report
scenarios.text: A reporter asks you, on the record, about the club's rookie traditions. There's a story going around the league about another club's hazing, and she wants to know about yours.

choices.label: Keep it to pastries and pads
choices.result: Pastries and pads, mostly, you explain, smiling. It's true, it's enough, and the captains notice you didn't give her anything else.

choices.label: Name the one that should change
choices.result: The one tradition that made you uncomfortable should change, you say carefully, without names. The captains agree, quietly, and change it.

choices.label: Keep the locker room private
choices.result: The locker room stays private, you say politely. She writes that the rookies 'declined to comment', and the story moves on.

scenarios.title: The Fan Who Sends Gifts
scenarios.text: A fan sends gifts to the facility every week, addressed to you: candy, then socks, then a framed painting of you as a medieval knight. The notes are getting longer.

choices.label: Tell security
choices.result: The club's security staff hears about it from you. They handle it kindly and firmly, and the knight painting goes in a storage room.

choices.label: Send one thank-you
choices.result: One thank-you note, warm and clear, asking them to stop sending gifts. It works, and you keep the painting, secretly.

choices.label: Ignore the gifts
choices.result: Ignored. The gifts keep coming, then the letters do, and by December you're a little uneasy every time the mailroom calls.

scenarios.title: Your First Endorsement Shoot
scenarios.text: Your first commercial shoot takes eleven hours in a warehouse for fifteen seconds of you holding a sports drink and saying one line. The director keeps saying 'more joy'.

choices.label: Nail every take
choices.result: Every take, nailed, with more joy each time. The director asks you back for the next campaign and calls you 'a natural', which is a lie.

choices.label: Make the crew laugh
choices.result: The crew, laughing between takes, is the best part of the day. The makeup artist gives you their number for the next shoot.

choices.label: Just survive it
choices.result: Survived, barely, eleven hours of 'more joy'. Your face hurts from smiling, you sleep in the car on the way home, and you never watch the ad.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Who Wants Your Spot
scenarios.text: An undrafted kicker in camp keeps showing up early and kicking where you can see: long ones, clean ones, every morning, with a little look over his shoulder.

choices.label: Show up earlier
choices.result: Earlier. He shows up earlier still. By the end of camp you're both kicking in the dark, and you've both gotten better.

choices.label: Give him a tip
choices.result: A tip about his plant foot, freely given. He thanks you sincerely and still wants your job, which you respect.

choices.label: Stay with your charts
choices.result: Your charts, your routine, nothing else. The coaches notice how calm you are while he keeps glancing over his shoulder at you.

scenarios.title: The First Time You Hear Boos
scenarios.text: Fans boo at a practice that's open to the public, after you miss two in a row in front of the bleachers. There are maybe three hundred people, and you know exactly who they mean.

choices.label: Answer with the next ten
choices.result: The next ten kicks go through. The boos stop somewhere around number six, and by number ten somebody in the bleachers is clapping.

choices.label: Wave at the boo section
choices.result: A big, friendly wave at the boo section. They laugh, and so do you, and one of them asks for an autograph after practice.

choices.label: Ask for a tool for crowd noise
choices.result: The team psychologist gives you one tool for crowd noise: a word, a breath, a spot on the ball. It works the next week.

scenarios.title: The Phone Call Home
scenarios.text: You call home every Sunday at six, and this Sunday, after a bad week, you don't know what to say. {parent} answers on the first ring, like always.

choices.label: Tell him the truth
choices.result: You're struggling, you tell him. {parent} says he's proud of you anyway, and the way he says it, you believe him for the first time in a month.

choices.label: Talk about anything else
choices.result: The weather, his garden, the neighbor's new fence: an hour of anything else but football. It helps more than you expected it to.

choices.label: Ask about his hardest year
choices.result: How did he get through his hardest year? He tells you, slowly, things you never knew, and you write it down after you hang up.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Paycheck Math
scenarios.text: Late one night you do the math on your rookie contract, on the back of an envelope: the average career, the taxes, the agent's cut. The number at the bottom is smaller than you thought.

choices.label: Make a five-year plan
choices.result: A five-year plan, made with your agent and an honest financial advisor. It's dull and comforting, like a good warmup.

choices.label: Make every season count
choices.result: Every season has to count, you decide, and you add an extra workout every week. The envelope goes on your fridge.

choices.label: Put the envelope away
choices.result: The envelope goes in a drawer, and you try not to think about it. You sleep less well than you'd like.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Who Calls Home Crying
scenarios.text: A rookie in your class calls home after every practice, in the parking lot, sometimes in tears. The veterans have started to notice, and one of them has started doing an impression.

choices.label: Sit with him at lunch
choices.result: Lunch together, every day. He calls home a little less and laughs a little more, and by November he's doing impressions of the veteran.

choices.label: Ask the veterans to ease up
choices.result: The veterans, asked quietly to ease up. One of them tells you about his own first year, when he called home every night too.

choices.label: Let him find his way
choices.result: He'll find his way, you decide, and you mind your own business. He makes it through, barely, and never quite trusts the room.

scenarios.title: Contract Year: Prove It
scenarios.text: It's the last year of your rookie deal, and the front office wants to see one more season before it talks numbers. Your agent says the word 'prove' three times in one phone call.

choices.label: Put your head down
choices.result: No contract talk, no reading, just kicking. Your agent handles the rest, and the season feels lighter for it, until the last month.

choices.label: Ask {coach} what they need
choices.result: {coach} gives you an honest answer in the hallway: two things, both fixable, neither about your leg. You fix them both by midseason, quietly.

choices.label: Push for a deal now
choices.result: An extension before the season, your agent asks. The club says no, politely, and you spend the season wondering if asking was a mistake.

scenarios.title: The Long-Distance Relationship
scenarios.text: {love_interest} is three states away, and your schedule doesn't have room for flights. Your calls have started ending with long silences neither of you knows how to fill.

choices.label: Fly them in for the bye
choices.result: A flight for the bye week, booked that night. It's short, and it's enough until the next one, and you both cry at the airport.

choices.label: Call every night at ten
choices.result: A video call every night at ten, no matter what. Some nights it's five minutes and a yawn, and it holds.

choices.label: Put the season first
choices.result: The season comes first, you explain, and you'll make it up in the offseason. {love_interest} says okay, too quickly, and hangs up first.
